title: Evidence to action
type: Retrospective qualitative synthesis; no evidence-strength scoring

cells.text: US interviews identified memory, progression and independence as desired outcomes.
Ye asked whether editing preserves normal apoE roles and changes cellular function.
Q8: 71/103 selected improvement compared with existing treatment.
Evaluation focus: connect editing with controlled cellular readouts; daily-life outcomes remain a future question.
Chinese care research and US treatment choices show that care context and stakeholder priorities matter.
Zhou raised repeat dosing and family burden; Dai considered delivery, cost and choice.
Q8 covered duration and cost, but did not measure appointments, monitoring or care hours.
Priority changed: give delivery burden greater attention; a future use and follow-up schedule remains to be defined.
Beijing interviews identified care-knowledge needs; the global report adds wider stigma concerns.
Ms. Wu raised small print, dense text and limited support time.
Q10: 51/103 selected vague effectiveness claims and 46/103 selected jargon; stigma was not assessed.
Implemented: shorter workbook text and larger app controls; planned: test comprehension with intended users.
Beijing primary care workers described workload and coordination barriers.
Shokz discussions did not establish a shared match of development resources and responsibilities.
Not assessed: partner resources, service capacity and wearable performance.
Route stopped: the Shokz partnership did not proceed; Anjia Guardian became a separate support tool.
